note: M1. Core fork: genetic/chromosome approach (vary-and-select whole schemas, reinforcement side) vs Sussman's propagator model (adapt within local constraints, society side). Introduces the performance landscape and fitness.

entities.name: adaptation
entities.definition: Learning to search effectively (where to search), framed as a population-level generate-and-test that assigns credit across spatially-interdependent actions; AI ideas for it are 'evolutionary strategies' derived from Darwinism.

entities.name: performance landscape
entities.definition: A picture of the relationship between an agent's actions (X-axis) and performance/fitness (elevation); used to visualize learning as a journey across hills, valleys, ridges, and mesas.

entities.name: fitness
entities.definition: A system's ability to survive and reproduce relative to others; performance is judged relative to a specific type of problem (a niche), not absolutely.

entities.name: genetic algorithm
entities.definition: Holland's approach: represent a solution as a chromosome of genes (bit strings), and adapt a population via crossover and mutation selected by fitness — searching a vast space by 'implicit parallelism', balancing exploration and exploitation.

entities.name: propagator model
entities.definition: Sussman's approach: represent a problem as connected objects (cells) carrying local constraints, and adapt by propagating information among them so each constraint can be satisfied independently — not by evolving a whole schema.

entities.name: John Holland
entities.definition: University of Michigan scholar who pioneered genetic algorithms and the insight of implicit parallelism.

entities.name: Gerald Sussman
entities.definition: Minsky's student at MIT who pioneered the propagator model for constraint-based adaptation and reasoning.

relations.evidence: Adaptation is a population-level generate-and-test strategy for assigning credit.
The landscape metaphor visualizes the feedback-driven adaptation process.
Adaptation assigns credit by selecting higher-fitness solutions.
Adaptation fleshes out the watchmaker parable's spatial decomposition of parts by function.
Climbing the wrong local peak on a rugged landscape visualizes superstitious learning.
Genetic algorithms are one evolutionary approach to adaptation.
The propagator model is the second evolutionary approach.
GAs balance exploration and exploitation just as reinforcement learning does.
Implicit parallelism works by balancing exploration-exploitation across a population.
The propagator model adapts within a society of connected constraint-bearing objects.
Minsky frames the propagator model as flexibly manipulating symbols to construct the landscape, closer to Simon's means-ends analysis.
Minsky's overall view of evolutionary strategies motivates the propagator model.

claims.proposition: Adaptation is a population-level generate-and-test strategy that assigns credit across spatially-interdependent actions, complementing reinforcement's focus on sequentially-interdependent actions.
Simple evolutionary operators — variation, selection, retention (VSR) — can adapt solutions to problems of vast complexity, as a competitive market 'learns' to select high-fitness firms.

On a rugged landscape, hill-climbing gets an agent stuck on a local peak (myopia, path dependence, superstitious learning); escaping requires exploration ('long-jumps') balanced against exploitation (hill-climbing).
claims.conditions: interdependence makes the landscape rugged with multiple local peaks

claims.proposition: Genetic algorithms search a vast space via 'implicit parallelism' — crossover and mutation over a population of chromosomes — extending reinforcement's exploration-exploitation balance with the simple abstraction of chromosomes.
claims.conditions: structure cannot be decomposed and can only be experimented with

claims.proposition: In the propagator model a problem is represented as connected objects carrying local constraints, and adaptation occurs within each constraint by propagating information among objects, rather than evolving an entire schema.
claims.conditions: the structure can be understood as stable constraints

claims.proposition: Minsky argued that gene- and chromosome-inspired approaches are too slow because they mostly hill-climb; intelligence instead needs to construct an understanding of a problem's structure as constraints, closer to means-ends analysis.
claims.conditions: problems where evolution would take too many generations

tensions.dimension: how to adapt on a rugged landscape: vary-and-select across whole schemas by balancing exploration/exploitation vs. propagate information within local constraints to construct an understanding of structure
tensions.conditions_a: The genetic approach fits when the designer cannot decompose a problem's structure and can only experiment: treat building blocks as genes/chromosomes and let variation and selection (implicit parallelism) explore the landscape — at the risk of being slow and merely hill-climbing.
tensions.conditions_b: The propagator model fits when structure can be understood as stable constraints: adapt within each constraint independently by propagating information among connected objects, smoothing the landscape — closer to Simon's means-ends analysis than to blind variation.

probes.prompt: On a rugged performance landscape, why does pure hill-climbing get an agent 'stuck', and how do exploration vs. exploitation address it? What does Minsky's 'mesa' landscape add that hills and peaks miss?
expected_signals: Explains that hill-climbing on a rugged landscape converges to a local (not global) peak — myopia and path dependence.
Frames exploitation as small hill-climbing moves and exploration as risky long-jumps to escape local peaks.
Connects climbing the wrong peak to superstitious learning (feedback that only seems to improve performance).
Notes the mesa landscape has no gradients, so the challenge is reaching a threshold of understanding ('giant strides'), not optimizing.
